meters.label: Elements copied by the worst append

frames.narration: Each request appends one event to the buffer, a dynamic array with room for 8. Seven appends cost one write each.
The ninth append finds the array full. It asks the allocator for room for 16 and copies 8 elements across. This one append costs 8 copies, the others none.
Over 100,000 appends the doubling policy makes 131,071 copies in total: 1.31 per append. The resizes get rarer as the array grows, so the append is O(1) amortized.

But one append copied 65,536 elements in a row. It is 17 appends out of 100,000, invisible in the average, and it lands on whichever request happened to be unlucky: a latency spike in the slowest 0.02%.

Someone changes the policy to add 10 slots each time. Every resize still copies the whole array, but now they come every 10 appends: 499,960,000 copies for 100,000 appends, about 5,000 per append. Growth by a constant is not amortized O(1).
A 1.5x factor sits in between: 276,521 copies, about 2.76 per append, with 29 resizes. A smaller factor leaves less unused memory and pays for it with more copying.

Shrinking has its own trap. An array of 1,025 items has capacity 2,048. If it halves whenever it is half empty, a remove and an append at that boundary copy 2,048 elements per cycle: 204,800 copies in 100 cycles. Shrinking at a quarter full makes it 0.
